## Motivation

![Gartner Magic Quadrant™ for Analytics & Business Intelligence Platforms](img/tableau-gartner.png){width="50%" height="50%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.notes}
Tableau (now part of Salesforce) has been up there as one of the leaders in analytics and BI for over 10 years. It is a very popular BI and dashboard product due to its relative ease of use, ability to handle largish data and having essentially good defaults to create good visualizations. 

It is a point-and-click software and hence reproducibility is a real challenge (much like Excel). But it can get a one-off
visualization and dashboard out very quickly. So it is good for interactive exploration and quick deep dives. 

:::

## Pros and cons
![](img/2023-02-13-11-09-02.png){width=800}
<!-- ## {background-image="img/tableau-pros-cons.png" background-size="contain"} -->

::: {.notes}
Tableau can access data from almost any local or cloud data store or database

It also creates responsive, mobile friendly graphics and dashboards
:::

## Measures, Dimensions and Attributes

Tableau uses these definitions:

-   A **measure** is a field that is a dependent variable; that is, its value is a function of one or more dimensions. Tableau treats any field containing numeric (quantitative) information as a **measure**. Measures can be aggregated.
-   A **dimension** is a field that can be considered an independent variable. By default, Tableau treats any field containing qualitative, categorical information as a **dimension**.
-   Another way to view a dimension is to treat it as an **Attribute**. Do this by choosing Attribute from the context menu for the dimension. The Attribute aggregation has several uses:
    -   It can ensure a consistent level of detail when blending multiple data sources.
    -   It can provide a way to aggregate dimensions when computing table calculations, which require an aggregate expression.
    -   It can improve query performance because it is computed locally.

## Measures and Dimensions

In simpler terms

-   Dimension role

    -   Qualitative fields
    -   Categorical variables
    -   Come out into view as themselves

-   Measure role

    -   Quantitative fields
    -   Come out into view as aggregates

Also, Tableau assumes that columns are fields, so it assumes **tidy data**

# Connecting Tableau to R & Python

## Connecting to analytic back ends {.smaller}

::: {.column width="47%"}
![](img/tableau-extensions.png){height="400"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
### Einstein Discovery

[Einstein Discovery](https://www.tableau.com/products/einstein-discovery) is a no-code ML product for predictive analytics that is a sister product to Tableau (under the Salesforce umbrella)
:::
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
-   Tableau provides an [open-source API](https://tableau.github.io/analytics-extensions-api/) that can be used to extend Tableau. Default services that connect are R, Python and MATLAB
    -   The {{< fa brands r-project >}} connection is through the `Rserve` package and service
    -   The {{< fa brands python >}} connection is through the [`TabPy`](https://tableau.github.io/TabPy/) package and service
        -   The {{< fa brands python >}} connection through the `TabPy` package can serve as middleware to connect with other services like AWS Sagemaker ([link](https://tableau.github.io/analytics-extensions-api/docs/ae_summary.html))
-   Tableau actually connects with these back ends using [`SCRIPT` functions](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/r_connection_manage.htm?source=productlink#script-functions-for-expressions)
:::

[[Tableau resource page](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/r_connection_manage.htm?source=productlink)]{.aside}

## Configure R and Rserve for Tableau use

1.  Install the `Rserve` package in your installation

``` r
install.packages("Rserve")
```

2.  Start the Rserve server

``` r
Rserve::Rserve(args="--no-save")
```

For running on your own machine, this is served on `localhost:6311`. However the Rserve instance can be deployed on a remote server, with or without SSL-encryption.

:::: { .absolute .bottom-2}
::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
If you don't include the `args` above, you **may** get an error from R

`Fatal error: you must specify ‘--save’, ‘--no-save’ or ‘--vanilla’`

## Configure Python and TabPy for Tableau use

Install `TabPy`. This is best done using `pip` and not `conda`. 

::: {.callout-caution icon=true appearance="simple"}
This can cause a bit of a problem down the line, so I'm actually going to set this up in a separate virtualenv so that my conda environment isn't damaged.

```bash
python3 -m venv ~/python-envs/tabpy_env
source ~/python-envs/tabpy_env/bin/activate
pip install tabpy
```
:::



This sets up `tabpy` as a service that can start at the command line

```bash
tabpy
```

and can be connected at `localhost:9004`.

## Configure Python and TabPy for Tableau use

In Tableau, we can configure this from the same dialog we used for Rserve, except we'll choose the TabPy option

![](img/tableau-extensions-py.png){width=400 top=150 left=100 .absolute}
![](img/tableau-py2.png){width=400 top=180 left=130 .absolute .fragment .fade-in }
:::

# Updating a Tableau visualization with clustering
Download workbooks: [ {{< fa download >}} {{< fa brands r-project >}} ](topics/tableau/anly503-r.twbx) | [{{< fa download >}} {{< fa brands python >}} ](topics/tableau/anly503-python.twbx)


## A basic visualization

We'll use an AirBNB dataset composed of all AirBNB properties in New York City that were listed on 1 September, 2015. 

::: {.tr}
[{{< fa download >}} Data](https://github.com/anly503/datasets/raw/main/airbnb.xlsx)
:::

- We will do a geospatial visualization by ZIP code
   - including summary information on price, number of beds and reviews ratings

## Connecting with R{.smaller}

- Make sure `Rserve` is running!!

We're going to create a Calculated Field, where the calculation will be in {{< fa brands r-project >}}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
![](img/tableau-r1.png)
:::
::: {.column width="47%"}
- We write R code directly in the Calculated Field window
- We wrap it in `SCRIPT_INT`
    - The output of the R script is an array of integers (cluster ids)
- In `SCRIPT_INT`, we specify the inputs from the Worksheet
    - If an input is a **measure** or continuous variable, it has to be input as an **aggregate**
    - The inputs are denoted in the R script as `.arg1`, `.arg2`, etc

#### [Useful resource!](https://www.tableau.com/sites/default/files/media/using-r-and-tableau-software_1.pdf){align="right"}
:::
::::
